title: Pollution and Eco-friendly Industry
tagline: Every source of pollution the syllabus names, the control measures that answer each, and the case for eco-friendly industrial development.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Commercial Applications syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (Examination Year 2027 and 2028 documents as reproduced by AglaSem, Scribd and Oswal Publishers; cisce.org returned 403). No board examination paper was consulted, every question is original practice, no figure is presented as an official statistic, and — as the syllabus itself requires — no question asks the student to record accounting entries or perform accounting calculations.

overview.intro: Unit 1(d) follows naturally from environmental awareness: if resources deplete, pollution degrades. The syllabus lists sources with unusual specificity — vehicular and industrial pollution, burning garbage, brick kilns, industrial waste, offshore oil drilling, thermal pollution, chemical fertiliser, biomedical waste, pesticides, and radiation including X-rays and nuclear fallout — and then asks for control measures and the need for eco-friendly industrial development. This chapter keeps that list intact, sorts each source into the medium it pollutes, teaches control at the source rather than at the end of the pipe, and closes with what makes an industry eco-friendly in commercial terms. The examiner rewards precision: a named source with a matching control outperforms a general paragraph about keeping rivers clean.

learningOutcomes: List the sources of pollution prescribed by the syllabus and classify each by medium.
Explain how vehicular, industrial and agricultural sources pollute air, water and soil.
Match a control measure to each source of pollution.
Describe thermal, biomedical and radiation pollution in outline.
Argue the commercial and environmental case for eco-friendly industrial development.

learn.title: Sources that foul the air: vehicles, industry, kilns and garbage

blocks.text: The syllabus opens its pollution list with the two largest urban sources. Vehicular pollution comes from engines burning petrol and diesel, which release carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides and fine particulates at street level, exactly where people breathe; a congested junction is therefore an air-quality problem before it is a traffic problem. Industrial pollution adds smokestack emissions — sulphur dioxide from burning coal, dust from grinding and cutting, and vapours from chemical processes — which travel with the wind and damage crops and buildings far from the plant. Brick kilns deserve separate mention because they burn coal and agricultural waste to fire clay, releasing smoke and particulates across a wide belt while the surrounding soil is stripped of its top layer. Burning garbage is the household-scale version of the same act: open piles set alight release dioxins and ash, and the plastic in them makes the smoke far more harmful than the paper. Offshore oil drilling adds a marine source — spillage and discharge during extraction spread oil over water, blocking light and air at the surface. Each source is airborne or waterborne, but all share one mechanism: something useful is burned or released without being contained.

blocks.caption: Air-polluting sources and what they release
rows: Carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides, particulates
Sulphur dioxide, smoke, dust, chemical vapours
Air over plants and downwind farmland
Spilled oil and discharge at sea

items: All these sources share a cause the syllabus names: irrational use of fuels without containment.
Air pollution crosses boundaries — a plant’s smoke becomes a district’s health cost.
Fuel choice is the first control point: cleaner fuel burns cleaner before any filter is fitted.

learn.title: Sources that foul water and soil: waste, fertiliser, pesticides and heat

blocks.text: Water and soil receive pollution in liquid and solid form. Industrial waste discharged into rivers carries oils, acids, dyes and heavy metals that kill fish and make the water unusable downstream; textile effluent is the standard example, colouring a river while poisoning its oxygen. Chemical fertiliser applied beyond what crops can absorb washes into rivers with rain, where it feeds algae growth that starves fish of oxygen, and it degrades soil structure over seasons. Pesticides are more persistent: sprays meant for insects settle on soil and leaves, enter the food chain, and concentrate as they climb it, which is why residues appear in milk and grain far from the field. Biomedical waste — used dressings, needles, syringes and laboratory cultures from hospitals — is dangerous out of proportion to its volume, because untreated material can transmit infection directly into soil or water when dumped. Thermal pollution is the quieter source: power stations and large plants return their cooling water to the river much hotter than they drew it, warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and organisms that survive the heat then suffocate. The pattern across all five is the same — a useful process ends with an untreated by-product released into a shared sink.

blocks.caption: Water and soil polluting sources with their control
rows: Oils, dyes and metals poison river life
Treatment plant before discharge; recover dyes and metals
Algae growth and oxygen loss in water; soil structure decline
Apply only the tested dose; compost and crop rotation
Toxins concentrate up the food chain
Infection transmitted through soil and water
Segregation, incineration and autoclaving at the source
Cooling towers; reuse heat instead of dumping it

learn.title: Radiation pollution: X-rays, nuclear fallout and their pathways

blocks.text: The syllabus groups radiation last, and it behaves unlike any other source because it cannot be seen, smelled or filtered out of a room by ordinary means. Two pathways are named. Diagnostic X-rays and medical radiation expose people directly; in controlled doses the benefit justifies the exposure, but unshielded or overused equipment adds needless dose to patients and staff. Radioactive fallout from nuclear plants and weapons testing is environmental: particles settle on soil and pasture, pass into milk and crops, and remain active for years because radioactive decay is not hurried by any cleanup method. Beyond these, industrial radiography and radioactive waste transport extend the risk along the supply chain. Radiation damages living tissue at the cellular level, which is why the controls are exclusion rather than dilution — shielding with lead or concrete, distance from the source, limiting time near it, and strict containment and monitoring of waste. Unlike smoke, diluting fallout does not make it safe; it only spreads it, a distinction that separates radiation control from every other control in this unit.

items.text: A hospital stores X-ray film and lead aprons, and rotates staff away from the exposure room.
items.note: Controls acting on time, shielding and distance — the three defences against radiation dose.

items.text: A nuclear plant’s cooling water is monitored before release, and waste is sealed in containers for controlled storage.
items.note: Containment rather than dilution, because spreading radioactive material does not reduce its activity.

learn.title: Control measures and the case for eco-friendly industry

blocks.text: Control works best where the pollution begins. At the source, a plant can change fuel, change raw material or change process — natural gas instead of coal, non-toxic solvents, closed loops that reuse water — so that less harm is created in the first place. Along the route, filters, scrubbers and settlers remove particulates and acids from smoke and effluent before release; electrostatic precipitators capture fine dust that ordinary filters miss. At the sink, treatment before discharge restores what the process disturbed: effluent is neutralised and aerated, garbage is segregated for composting and recycling rather than burning, and biomedical waste is incinerated or autoclaved at the hospital itself. Eco-friendly industrial development is the design that puts all three together: an industry organised so that inputs are clean, processes are efficient, waste is treated and, wherever possible, recycled back into production. The commercial argument is as strong as the environmental one. Treated material that is reused is material not bought; a plant that discharges clean effluent avoids closure orders; a manufacturer whose product can be recycled keeps customers in a market that increasingly asks the question. The syllabus’s phrase “need for eco-friendly industrial development” is therefore an economic need as well as an ecological one, and an exam answer that shows both sides is complete.

blocks.caption: The three control points
rows: Biogas instead of coal; closed-loop water
Effluent treatment; composting instead of burning

items: Prevention costs less than cure: a closed loop saves the purchase of fresh material as well as the treatment bill.
Recycling turns a waste cost into an input, which is the commercial meaning of eco-friendly.
Compliance protects continuity — a plant ordered closed loses every day of production.

keyPoints: Vehicular pollution releases carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and particulates at street level.
Industrial smoke carries sulphur dioxide, dust and vapours that damage crops downwind.
Burning garbage is especially harmful because plastics in it release dioxins.
Industrial effluent carries oils, dyes and heavy metals that poison river life.
Excess fertiliser causes algae growth that depletes oxygen in water.
Pesticides concentrate as they move up the food chain.
Biomedical waste must be segregated and destroyed at the source, not dumped.
Thermal pollution lowers dissolved oxygen because warm water holds less of it.
Radiation is controlled by shielding, distance and time — not by dilution.
Eco-friendly industry uses clean inputs, clean processes and treated, recycled waste.
examFocus: “List the sources of pollution” — reproduce the prescribed list, then group them by air, water or soil for full marks.
“Suggest measures to control pollution” — pair every source with a matching control; unpaired suggestions score poorly.
“What is the need for eco-friendly industrial development?” — give the environmental reason and the commercial reason, with a worked example of recycling inside a plant.

vocabulary.meaning: The introduction of harmful substances or energy into the environment faster than it can be absorbed.
The discharge of heated water or air into the environment, lowering dissolved oxygen in water.
Contaminated material from hospitals and laboratories that can transmit infection if dumped.
Radioactive particles released into the air that settle on soil, water and crops.
Liquid waste discharged from a plant, which must be treated before release.
Industry organised so that its inputs, processes and waste harm the environment as little as possible.
Processing used material back into usable input instead of discarding it.
Synthetic plant nutrient applied to soil, harmful in excess through water run-off.

questions.prompt: The discharge of hot cooling water into a river is an example of:
questions.explanation: Hot water raises the river’s temperature and reduces its dissolved oxygen, which suffocates aquatic life — the definition of thermal pollution.
questions.commonMistake: Fertiliser run-off also lowers oxygen, but through algae growth; heat does it directly.

questions.prompt: Which prescribed source is controlled by incineration or autoclaving at the point of origin?
options: Thermal discharge from a power station
Chemical fertiliser washed off a field
questions.explanation: Infected material must be destroyed where it is generated — by high-temperature incineration or steam autoclaving — because transporting it spreads the hazard.
questions.commonMistake: The other three sources are controlled by fuel choice, cooling systems and dose control respectively.

questions.prompt: Radioactive fallout is unlike other pollutants mainly because:
options: Diluting or spreading it does not make it safe; only shielding, distance and time reduce exposure
It disappears when mixed with river water
questions.answer: Diluting or spreading it does not make it safe; only shielding, distance and time reduce exposure
questions.explanation: Radioactivity is not destroyed by dilution — spreading fallout distributes it over more ground and more people, so control must exclude it through lead or concrete shielding, distance and limited time.
questions.commonMistake: Do not apply the “dilution is the solution” logic of effluent to radiation.

questions.prompt: A textile dyeing unit that recovers dye from its effluent and reuses it is applying which principle?
options: Recycling at the source, which cuts both pollution and purchase cost
questions.answer: Recycling at the source, which cuts both pollution and purchase cost
questions.explanation: Recovering dye before it leaves the plant prevents the pollution and removes the need to buy replacement dye — the dual commercial and environmental gain that defines eco-friendly practice.
questions.commonMistake: The waste never reaches the treatment stage, so this is prevention rather than end-of-pipe treatment.

questions.prompt: Hospitals must destroy used dressings, needles and cultures by incineration or autoclaving because such ______ waste can transmit infection if it is dumped.
questions.explanation: Biomedical waste carries infections, so it has to be destroyed at the hospital itself through high-temperature incineration or steam autoclaving rather than mixed with ordinary refuse.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer “industrial” — the waste comes from hospitals and laboratories and is dangerous out of proportion to its volume.

questions.prompt: Name two sources of water pollution and one control measure for each.
questions.answer: Industrial effluent carrying dyes and metals — controlled by an effluent treatment plant that neutralises and aerates the waste before discharge. Chemical fertiliser washed off fields — controlled by applying only the tested dose and using compost and crop rotation to maintain soil fertility.
questions.explanation: Each source is paired with a control that acts on it directly: treatment before release for effluent, and reduced input for fertiliser run-off.
questions.commonMistake: Controls must match the source; “plant more trees” does not address either mechanism.

questions.prompt: Explain how vehicular pollution harms health in a congested city.
questions.answer: Engines burning petrol and diesel release carbon monoxide, unburnt hydrocarbons, nitrogen oxides and fine particulates. In congested traffic these accumulate at street level, where pedestrians and roadside residents breathe them continuously. Carbon monoxide reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity, particulates irritate the lungs, and nitrogen oxides aggravate respiratory illness, so prolonged exposure raises the incidence of breathing problems among people who live and work near busy roads.
questions.explanation: The answer names the emissions, explains why congestion concentrates them at breathing height, and links each to a health effect rather than stopping at “it is harmful”.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop at listing gases — the mechanism of harm at street level is the marked part.

questions.prompt: Describe how industrial waste pollutes water and explain two measures to control it.
questions.answer: Industrial waste pollutes water when factories discharge untreated effluent into rivers and drains. Such effluent carries oils that form films blocking re-aeration, acids and alkalis that alter pH, dyes that stop light reaching aquatic plants, and heavy metals that poison fish and enter the food chain. The result is a river that loses its oxygen, its life and its usefulness for drinking or irrigation downstream. Two controls: first, an effluent treatment plant at the factory, where the waste is screened, settled, neutralised to a safe pH and aerated before release, removing most solids and toxicity; second, recovery and reuse inside the process, where dyes, oils and metals are extracted and returned to production so they never enter the effluent at all. The first controls what leaves, the second prevents what would leave, and together they meet the syllabus’s requirement for eco-friendly practice.
questions.explanation: The mechanism of harm is stated first with its consequences, then two controls at different points are described as processes, which is what “describe and explain” demands.
questions.commonMistake: A control list without the mechanism shows no understanding of why each control works.

questions.prompt: What is meant by eco-friendly industrial development? State any three features of an eco-friendly plant.
questions.answer: Eco-friendly industrial development means organising industry so that its operations cause the least possible harm to the environment while remaining commercially viable — pollution is designed out of the process instead of being cleaned up afterwards. Three features: first, clean inputs, where the plant substitutes renewable or less harmful materials, such as biogas or recycled fibre, for scarce or dirty ones; second, efficient processes that use water, energy and material in closed loops, so waste is minimised and cost falls with consumption; third, treatment and recycling, where every effluent and by-product is treated before release and recovered where possible to re-enter production. Such a plant also segregates waste at the source and monitors its emissions continuously. The design is judged both ecologically — less harm — and commercially — lower input cost, fewer closures and customers who prefer responsible suppliers.
questions.explanation: The definition frames pollution prevention rather than cleanup, and each feature is given with its mechanism and its commercial effect, which is the standard the syllabus sets for the topic.
questions.commonMistake: Planting trees alone is not eco-friendly industry; the features must change inputs, processes and waste handling.

questions.prompt: A sugar mill burns bagasse inefficiently, discharges its spent wash into a stream and sells the filter cake that accumulates on its yard. Classify each of these three practices as polluting or eco-friendly, and suggest a rearrangement that makes the mill eco-friendly.
questions.answer: Burning bagasse inefficiently is polluting: bagasse is the fibre left after crushing cane, and incomplete combustion sends smoke and particulates into the air while wasting fuel that could have been burned completely for steam. Discharging spent wash into the stream is polluting: it is a dark, acidic, high-BOD liquid that strips oxygen from the water and kills fish downstream. Selling the filter cake is eco-friendly in direction — a solid by-product leaves the yard as a useful product rather than a dump — though leaving it piled in the open still contaminates soil and rainwater. The rearrangement uses the mill’s own material flows: burn bagasse completely in a properly designed boiler, so it supplies steam without smoke; evaporate and treat the spent wash so its solids become additional filter cake and the water is neutralised before any discharge; and market every kilogram of filter cake as fertiliser rather than stockpiling it, which turns the yard into a warehouse. With these changes the mill runs on its own residue, releases only treated water, and converts all three waste streams into saleable or reusable output — the syllabus’s eco-friendly model, achieved without stopping production.
questions.explanation: Each practice is judged separately with the mechanism behind the judgement, then a single redesign reuses all three streams, which is the application-plus-evaluation structure an analytical question tests.
questions.commonMistake: Do not call all three polluting or all three green — the question deliberately mixes directions to test judgement.
